title: Big O in one minute (a race through a million names)
description:
Byte races Compy to find one name in a million. Big O is just how the work grows when the list grows.

#coding #python #bigo #shorts
angle: Big O does not measure seconds, it measures how the amount of work grows as the input grows.
hook: Ever wondered why some code is fast and some is painfully slow?

scenes.speaker: byte
scenes.narration: Ever wondered why some code is fast and some is painfully slow?

scenes.speaker: compy
scenes.narration: Stick around. One idea will change how you look at slow code.

props.heading: In this episode
items: A race through a million names

scenes.speaker: byte
scenes.narration: Race. I find one name in a million names. I start at the top and check every single one.

scenes.speaker: compy
scenes.narration: That could take a million steps. I'll just cut the list in half each time.

scenes.speaker: byte
scenes.narration: Twenty steps. You win by a mile. I'd ask for a rematch, but I'm scared of the result.

scenes.speaker: compy
scenes.narration: That gap is Big O. It's not about seconds. It's about how the work grows as the list grows.

props.code:
# one by one: O(n)
# halve each time: O(log n)

scenes.speaker: byte
scenes.narration: So if the list doubles, my way takes twice as long, and yours takes one extra step?

scenes.speaker: compy
scenes.narration: Yes. Don't trust me. Ask Python how many halvings a million needs.

scenes.speaker: byte
scenes.narration: Twenty. A million items, twenty steps. That feels illegal.

scenes.speaker: compy
scenes.narration: Rule of the day: ask how the work grows, not how long it takes.

scenes.speaker: byte
scenes.narration: That's it. Follow for more. Next up: git, the undo button for code.

claims.text: Binary search finds an item in a sorted list in O(log n) time by halving the search range
Big O notation describes how an algorithm's work grows with input size
